title: Friction-to-Outcome Mapping: ML / Backend / Platform Audience Talktracks
body:
Objective:
Quick reference for SDRs, AMs, and demo engineers: map common friction points -> desired outcomes -> concise talktracks for ML engineers, backend engineers, and platform teams. Lightweight competitive notes and suggested demo hooks included.

Notes on tone:
- ML engineers: technical, care about model fidelity, latency tail, eval regressions, and reproducibility. Mention evals, token economics, caching semantics.
- Backend engineers: reliability-first, SLOs, observability, predictable cost. Use latency percentiles, autoscale behavior, and rollback stories.
- Platform teams: integration, policy/cost controls, infra portability, multitenancy. Show policy routing, VPC/private, KMS/HSM integrations.

High-level friction -> outcome mappings (one-liners to use live):
- Friction: "Latency spikes during peak inference" -> Outcome: "Stable P99 under SLO via smart routing + burst pools" -> TL;DR: "We route by latency SLO, fall back to compatible quantized variants and burst capacity so your P99 stays bounded."
- Friction: "Costs explode on dense traffic" -> Outcome: "Unit cost reduction via batching + prefix/KV cache" -> TL;DR: "Automatic batching + prefix caching reduces per-token cost without changing prompts; customers see 2–5x token efficiency on chat-heavy flows."
- Friction: "Models regress after upstream updates" -> Outcome: "Controlled rollouts and eval gating" -> TL;DR: "Pin model versions, run A/B evals against your golden prompts and automated regression alerts before traffic shifts."
- Friction: "Can't expose customer data to hosted vendors" -> Outcome: "VPC/private deployments with customer-managed keys" -> TL;DR: "Private control plane or on-prem package, with audit logs and KMS integration."

Persona-specific talktracks (short scripts you can memorize):
1) ML Engineers (MLE) — 45–90s
- Hook: "If you treat inference as experiments, you need tight fidelity controls + reproducible evaluation. Redwood makes rollouts, model-variant testing, and prompt-based regression detection first-class."
- What to say: "You can pin model versions per route and attach an eval suite; any candidate model is run against your golden prompt set and quality metrics are surfaced before it sees production traffic."
- Evidence: "We keep token-level diffs, sample-level anomalies, and can alert on objective drift (e.g., BLEU/ROUGE/LM-agnostic scores). Try the eval-runner demo with your 50 prompts — we show per-prompt regression heatmaps in <2 minutes>."
- Demo hook: "Upload 20 prompts and a baseline model; show a canary rollout (5% -> 25% -> 100%) while monitoring quality and latency panels. Point out the auto-fallback policy."
- FAQ handle: "If they press: 'But latency increases with larger contexts' — answer: 'We pick kernel paths by seq-length distribution and can suggest quantization/batching tradeoffs; also prefix caching reduces repeat-token costs.'"

2) Backend Engineers — 30–60s
- Hook: "You want predictable SLOs and cost, not just model bells and whistles."
- What to say: "Redwood lets you set route-level SLOs and enforces them through routing policies and capacity tiers. When capacity is tight we do compatible fallback (smaller quantized variant) rather than failing hard."
- Evidence: "Operations teams report 3x fewer P1 incidents related to inference during releases because Canary + automatic fallback avoids saturation cascades."
- Demo hook: "Show the console route where you set P95/P99 targets and the simulated traffic test that triggers auto-fallback. Toggle a sudden 10x traffic spike and show the system holding latency while slightly changing model variant."
- FAQ handle: "'How do you avoid noisy neighbors on shared infra?' — answer: 'Dedicated pools and strict isolation for reserved capacity; when on shared, we use eviction policies and QoS shims.'"

3) Platform Teams — 60–120s
- Hook: "If you need consistent inference across self-hosted, dedicated, and hosted fleets with centralized policy, Redwood provides a single abstraction layer."
- What to say: "Single API, same rollout and observability primitives across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. You can enforce routing by region, cost center, or compliance label from one control plane."
- Evidence: "Case: exchange platform moved from fragmented model endpoints to one abstracted route and reclaimed 25% of spend via optimized routing + quantized model variants per region."
- Demo hook: "Show policy editor: create a rule (eu-only -> private cluster, high-sensitivity routes -> private KMS) and show audit trail + role-based access controls."
- FAQ handle: "'What about audits and export controls?' — answer: 'We surface per-request audit logs and integrate with your SIEM; private deployments can be air-gapped.'"

Competitive notes (short bullets to deploy in calls):
- Large cloud AI endpoints (big public clouds): strength = breadth + managed infra. Weakness = less inference-specific knobs: no integrated prefix caching, limited canary/eval tooling for ML quality, and vendor lock for private deployments.
- Inference runtimes / self-hosted vendors (e.g., OSS runtime stacks): strength = control and cost potential. Weakness = operational burden; missing a packaged control plane for rollouts, evals, and enterprise RBAC.
- Other LLM API providers: strength = fast onboarding. Weakness = limited dedicated/private path + fewer low-level performance levers (kernel selection, smart KV cache) that reduce unit cost at scale.

Tactical rebuttals to common competitive claims:
- Claim: 'We can host the model ourselves and save money.' Rebuttal: 'Maybe; but total cost of ownership includes SRE time, regression testing, and the tooling to safely scale. Our customers tell us integrated evals + rollout automation was the single biggest time-saver.'
- Claim: 'Cloud provider endpoints are simpler.' Rebuttal: 'For small proof of concepts yes; for production you want predictable P99, cost controls, and compliance. Redwood gives simple APIs for POC and the controls for production.'

Measurement hooks (what to surface in trial/POC to prove value):
- Latency: P50/P95/P99 before vs after routing/fallback changes (show graph)
- Cost: $/1M tokens with and without caching + batching
- Quality: % of prompts with regression flags during a model swap; user-facing error-category rate (hallucination/formatting)
- Ops MTTR: number of incidents related to inference during last release window

Collateral / quick assets to offer in outreach:
- 1-page: "Inference economics cheat sheet" (show batching/caching/quantization impact)
- Live demo script: "50 prompts, canary, simulated traffic spike" (5–8 min)
- Template: "Golden prompt set for evals" (20–50 example prompts across categories)

Open questions / things to iterate on (for GTM squad):
- Do we need separate cheat sheets for finance vs platform? Early feedback says yes — platform wants policy+audit; finance wants unit economics.
- Pilot pack: include a sample model and 20 golden prompts for MLEs to run instantly without data egress concerns.
- Pricing talk: create simple side-by-side comparison (hosted API unit price vs dedicated commit) to use when customers ask about committed savings.

Immediate next steps (this doc owner):
- [ ] Build 1 pager: inference economics (Evan)
- [ ] Draft demo script + recording of 6-min POC (Maya)
- [ ] Add 3 real customer examples (anonymized) showing latency/cost wins (Diego)

Rough follow-up timeline:
- Week 1: finalize 1-pager and demo script
- Week 2: pilot with Solutions Eng on 3 prospects and collect feedback

Raw snippets for Slack/LinkedIn outreach (copyable):
- "Experimenting with inference in prod? Try a canary with a pinned model + eval suite — Redwood can run your 50 prompts and flag regressions before traffic hits users."
- "Drop-in fallback when capacity bursts — keeps your P99 bounded and saves you from pager noise during launches."

Unresolved conversational points to take to product:
- How to present multi-model cost tradeoffs (e.g., mix of Llama2/Redwood-verified OPT variants) in a single UI card?
- Can the console auto-generate suggested golden prompts from a sample corpus?

End of draft.

(Informal: expect phrasing to be choppy in parts — this is a working doc intended to spawn collateral. Reuse or adapt language freely.)
